Activities and Experiences
The best thing to do at Jnane Rumi is to simply soak in the atmosphere. After a busy few days shuttling around the city, I found that all I wanted to do was stay still. I spent my two days there reading, walking among the fig, olive, and pistachio trees, admiring the property's incredible art collection, or napping in the shade by my pool, with birdsong nudging me awake.

If you do wish to explore Marrakesh, the property can organize exclusive artist studio visits and private architectural tours.

A cozy interior space with armchairs a couch and decor featuring a framed image of two individuals on a rear wall
Art by Mous Lamrabat, in a guest suite.
David Dumon/Jnane Rumi
The Spa
The hotel has a small hammam, and massage treatments are also available. I found it to be peaceful and very private—the spaces are really designed for one person, or perhaps a couple, so guests have the spa essentially to themselves.

Luxurious bathroom with a carved stone tub a towel draped over the edge and open windows revealing a palm tree and greenery outside
A deep soaking tub in the Sanai Suite's bathroom.
Jnane Rumi
Accessibility and Sustainability
Accessible spaces include the main garden, the rooftop bar, the living room, and the dining room. Guests with mobility challenges may want to consider booking the Annex or Pavilion rooms, which are ground-level, rather than the main house, which has stairs but no elevators.

On the sustainability front, Jnane Rumi maintains organic gardens and green spaces (using water-saving systems to be mindful of the desert environment) and supplies the restaurant with seasonal and locally sourced ingredients. The property also works with local designers and artisans for its art and furniture.

The outdoor bar and lounge.
Jnane Rumi
Location
The property is near the Palmeraie—a palm tree oasis planted in the 11th century—about a 15-20 minute drive from the heart of Marrakesh, including key sites like the medina, the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, and the Bahia Palace.

The 414-mile ‘Highway on Top of the World’ Is One of the Most Scenic Drives in the U.S.—and It Crosses the Arctic Circle
Get ready for unforgettable Alaskan landscapes.

By Bailey Berg 
Published on June 21, 2026
Leave a Comment
In This Article
Best Time to Drive
Know Before You Go
Stops Along the Route
A long straight road stretching through a forested valley with distant mountains under a cloudy sky
Alaska's Dalton Highway stretching into the distance.
Credit: Boyang Jin/500px/Getty Images
The Dalton Highway stretches 414 miles from near Fairbanks to Deadhorse through some of the most remote terrain in North America.
Travelers can experience the Yukon River, Arctic Circle, Brooks Range, Atigun Pass, abundant wildlife, and Arctic tundra landscapes.
Careful preparation is essential due to limited fuel, almost nonexistent cell service, harsh conditions, and active truck traffic.
Most road trips are built around convenience and roadside sites. The Dalton Highway almost seems designed to reject both of those things—but it makes up for it with some of the scenic landscapes and views that you can find in the U.S.

Stretching 414 miles from just outside Fairbanks, Alaska, to the Arctic oil-field outpost of Deadhorse, Alaska, the route cuts through some of the most remote terrain in North America: threading through black spruce forests, over mountain passes, and across vast tundra. Originally built in the 1970s to support construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, the road—commonly called the “Haul Road” by Alaskans—remains a working industrial corridor for truckers hauling freight to Prudhoe Bay oil fields. But over the years, it’s also gained a reputation for being an incredible road trip—one known in equal parts for delivering ruggedly beautiful landscapes and humbling those who underestimate it. It’s since earned another nickname: “The Highway on Top of the World.”

“On the Dalton Highway, you’re surrounded by nothing but nature—vast landscapes of tundra and treeless areas,” says Kathy Hedges of Northern Alaska Tour Company, which has been operating tours on the road for nearly 40 years. “One can get out and stand along the shores of the mighty Yukon River, cross the Continental Divide, or get out on the Arctic Coastal plains if they go all the way north.”  

Frank Stelges, an aurora photographer who has driven the Dalton more times than he can count, echoed that sentiment. “The landscape is so wide, and the sky is so blue and high,” he says. “You see so much wildlife left and right with bears and wolves and caribou and millions of birds. It’s just a super precious thing we have here in Alaska.” 

Stelges, originally from Germany, was so moved by his first motorcycle trip on the Dalton Highway that he decided to relocate to Alaska. Still, he added that he cautions travelers, thinking it’ll be a casual drive. 

“It’s not super long, less than 450 miles from Fairbanks, so probably what Texans drive for a coffee on a Sunday afternoon, but there is not much in between, right?” Stelges says. “There’s no cell phone reception, few gas stations, and when there’s a real emergency, you have to rely on yourself. You should be prepared for everything.” 

Here’s what you need to know about roadtripping the Dalton Highway. 

Best Time to Drive
A scenic highway with a bridge crossing a winding river in a mountainous forest landscape
Aerial View of the Dalton Highway during the summer.
Jacob/Adobe Stock
The Dalton Highway is technically open year-round, but for most travelers, the realistic window is mid-June through early September. Snow has typically melted from higher elevations like Atigun Pass, daylight stretches nearly around the clock, and temperatures are milder. July tends to offer the greenest landscapes and best wildlife viewing, while late August and early September bring tundra fall colors that turn the North Slope shades of crimson and gold.

June and July also bring mosquitoes in astonishing numbers, especially near wetlands and tundra pullouts. A strong bug spray is essential.

Driving the Dalton in winter is an entirely different category of trip. Temperatures can plunge to -40 degrees Fahrenheit or lower, daylight becomes limited (if not nonexistent, in the more northern latitudes), and storms can make for poor visibility. Yet some travelers specifically seek it out for that reason. In winter, the road becomes quieter, the tundra turns starkly beautiful, and the northern lights are often spectacular. Truckers still regularly drive the route, but conditions demand serious preparation, winter driving experience, and emergency planning. 

“When I go in winter, I have a really full survival kit with heavy sleeping bags, my Arctic gear (and not just a winter puffy jacket, but stuff where I can survive in 40 below), enough food for several days, and a generator to have the possibility to jump start my car in case something happens with the batteries,” Stelges says. 

The Alaska Department of Transportation notes that conditions are difficult year-round and that travelers should be prepared for long stretches without assistance. 

Know Before You Go
Motorcyclists traveling on a curved road through a forested area with light fog in the distance
A group of motocyclists along the Dalton Highway.
Jia Liu/Getty Images
Fuel and Services Are Extremely Limited
This is the most important thing to understand before setting out. There are essentially only three reliable fuel stops along the route: the Yukon River crossing, Coldfoot, and Deadhorse. The stretch between Coldfoot and Deadhorse is roughly 240 miles with virtually no services in between.

Drivers should start with a full tank, carry extra fuel if their range is limited, and bring emergency food, water, and warm clothing.  

Most Rental Cars Aren’t Allowed
The Daltons’ mix of gravel, sharp rocks, potholes, and heavy truck traffic has a reputation for destroying windshields and tires. For that reason, many standard rental car companies prohibit travel on the Dalton Highway. If you plan to drive it yourself, look for Alaska-based rental outfits that specifically allow Dalton travel and often include extras like emergency equipment. Hedges also recommends having at least one full-sized tire. “There is no maintenance along the highway, so they need to be prepared to change it themselves—or know a tow from Fairbanks will likely cost over $1,000,” she says. 

Stelges, meanwhile, recommends two tires—and knowing how to change them yourself. “If you have a serious accident, probably a truck will stop, but for just a flat tire, nobody will stop,” he says.  “So bring spare tires and a patch kit that you can use to get yourself back.” 

Expect Truck Traffic
The Dalton is still an active industrial supply road servicing Prudhoe Bay oil operations. Truckers have the right of way here, and you’ll share the route with massive semis hauling freight north. Slow down when trucks approach to minimize windshield damage from flying rocks, and avoid stopping in narrow sections or blind curves.

Cell Service Is Almost Nonexistent
Once you leave Fairbanks, expect long stretches without signal. Download offline maps before departure and don’t count on being able to call for help.

Related Stories
Best Times to Visit Alaska
A whale's tail out of the water with snowy mountains in the background in Juneau
My Late Father and I Planned to Go Fishing Together—Here's How I Fulfilled His Dream of Catching a King Salmon
Left a hand points to a map of Alaska Right a woman wearing an outdoor hat and gear is pictured in profile near a coastline
Stops Along the Route
Arctic Circle landmark sign surrounded by trees and a dirt path
The sign for the Arctic Circle in Alaska.
Galyna Andrushko/Adobe Stock
Yukon River Bridge
About 140 miles north of Fairbanks, this is one of the Dalton’s first major landmarks—and one of the few places to fuel up. The steel bridge spans 2,295 feet across the Yukon and parallels the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, which repeatedly appears and disappears beside the road throughout the trip. There’s also a small truck stop-style café that makes for an essential break before heading farther north—and a good place to get updates from fellow travelers about the road conditions. 

Arctic Circle Sign
Reaching the Arctic Circle is the milestone many travelers come for. The sign marking latitude 66°33’ north has become one of Alaska’s most photographed roadside attractions, and there’s usually a rotating cast of muddy trucks, rental RVs, and adventure motorcyclists posing for photos beside it. But the stop matters for more than just bragging rights. Depending on the season, this is where you officially enter the land of the midnight sun or polar night.

Coldfoot
Coldfoot is the Dalton Highway’s closest thing to a hub. Originally a mining camp during the gold rush, it now serves as a critical service stop with fuel, lodging, and meals.  The visitor center is worth more than a quick stop—rangers there can offer information on wildlife activity, weather conditions, hiking opportunities, and current road updates —and there are exhibits that explain both the region’s ecology and the complex history of Arctic development. Many travelers overnight here before attempting the long push to Deadhorse, especially because the next stretch—roughly 240 miles north—is even more isolated.

Wiseman
Just 13 miles north of Coldfoot, Wiseman feels like stepping into a different era of Alaska. This tiny historic village, home to only a small year-round population, began as a mining community in the early 1900s and still has a deeply off-grid feel. Several residents offer homestays or guided experiences, and the surrounding Brooks Range scenery is spectacular. Here and Coldfoot are also some of the best places on the route to potentially see the northern lights later in the season.

Just outside Wiseman, travelers will also find Arctic Hive, an off-grid retreat center that hosts yoga retreats, northern lights wellness trips, hiking excursions, and dog-mushing experiences from a cluster of cabins and geodesic domes overlooking the Brooks Range.

Atigun Pass
At 4,739 feet, Atigun Pass is the highest highway pass in Alaska, maintained year-round and one of the most dramatic sections of the drive. The road climbs steeply into the Brooks Range before descending onto the North Slope tundra. Dall sheep are commonly spotted here, clinging to impossibly steep cliffsides. 

Deadhorse
The Dalton Highway officially ends in Deadhorse, an oil-field settlement built to support operations at Prudhoe Bay. It’s not scenic in the traditional sense—expect gravel lots, modular buildings, and heavy equipment. During the summer, those who have made it all the way to Deadhorse have the option to purchase a shuttle to get them through the security gate of the Prudhoe Bay Oil Fields and dip their toes in the Arctic Ocean (or take a full dip if they are interested); however, this must be booked in advance at Deadhorse Camp’s website.

But for most travelers, the goal of the drive is simply reaching the top of the continent by road (before turning around and doing it all again in reverse).

Amazon Has a Tiny Home-style, 2-room Inflatable Glamping Tent That Fits 10 People and Comes With a Skylight
This canvas shelter will transform your backyard into a luxurious oasis.

By Olivia Young 
Published on June 21, 2026 06:30AM EDT
Leave a Comment
A glamping tent setup with two people seated by a campfire surrounded by a natural outdoor setting
Credit: Travel + Leisure / Amazon
Amazon has a $430 inflatable tent that can turn any yard or campsite into a luxurious glamping oasis in minutes.
With two bedrooms, a skylight, and a covered outdoor space, it offers plenty of room for groups of up to 10 people.
The Yoleny tent eschews traditional poles for an air-filled frame, making it easier to travel with and set up.
You don’t have to spend a fortune at a glamping resort in order to relish a picture-perfect night under the stars. With an under-$450 inflatable tent from Amazon, you can create a luxurious sleepout anywhere—including in your backyard.

Whether you opt to transport it to a scenic spot or set it up right in your garden, this 10-person home-away-from-home elevates the entire camping experience. For the price of one weekend at a high-end glamping resort in the Pocono Mountains or the California coast, you could have your own portable outdoor oasis to pack up and take wherever you go.

Yoleny 10-person Inflatable Glamping Tent
yoleny Inflatable Camping Tent
Credit: Amazon
$430 at Amazon
The Yoleny inflatable tent in question is roughly 13.5 feet wide and has a 6.5-foot-tall ceiling at its highest point. The side has an awning held up by support bars, which shades the front doorway and mesh window. Inside, you have two distinct spaces divided by a canvas wall—this can be used to separate the bedroom from the living space or split a large group between two rooms. The 180-square-foot tent can sleep up to 10 people at once; for reference, that’s almost as big as the average tiny home.

Amazon's Selling a Tiny Home-style Inflatable Glamping Tent That Fits 6 People—and It Sets Up in Minutes
It’s spacious and, yes, totally Instagram-worthy, but perhaps its most appealing selling point is how easy it is to set up. Instead of cumbersome stakes and poles, the tent obtains its shape with just air. The frame is a network of interconnecting thermoplastic polyurethane columns that you inflate with a manual pump, which comes included in the $430 price. A reviewer wrote that the tent can shift from rolled up and packed away to standing and sturdy within minutes.

It’s “an innovative and practical solution for outdoor enthusiasts seeking a spacious, easy-to-set-up shelter,” they continued. “This tent stands out for its unique inflatable design, which significantly simplifies the setup process compared to traditional pole tents.” Another customer who called it “durable and comfortable” says that it’s so good, it’ll be “the last tent you’ll ever buy.”

The brand calls this a four-season tent because it can hold up in a range of weather conditions. The durable Oxford cloth it’s made of has a waterproof PVC coating, and it has a fixed reinforcing layer of mesh that prevents rips and tears. In summer temperatures, the heat can escape through a number of ventilation ports. In the cold, you can warm the space with a wood stove, since the roof has a patch of flame-retardant fabric designed to be cut around a chimney.

Other attractive features include built-in storage pockets, lantern hooks, roll-up curtains, and skylights that beckon you to stretch out under the stars. One fun hack for family camping trips is to put the awning down and use it as a big screen for movies with a portable projector.

Surprisingly, this is just one of many inflatable tents on Amazon that could transform your backyard into a glamorous glamping hideaway. The options range from a $200 blow-up stargazing tent to an $850 mini mansion that sleeps 12. Find other shopper favorites, below.

7 U.S. Mountain Towns Where You Can Still Buy a Vacation Home for Under $400,000
According to Zillow, you can still find affordable homes in these mountain destinations across the U.S.

By Lydia Mansel 
Published on June 21, 2026
Leave a Comment
An old mining structure with a mountainous backdrop in a town setting
Overlooking downtown Butte, Montana.
Credit: DenisTangneyJr/Getty Images
As a travel writer who spends a significant amount of time in mountain towns—from Jackson, Wyoming, and Vail, Colorado, to Highlands, Cashiers, and Boone, North Carolina—I’m intimately familiar with the appeal of these types of destinations. They’ve all got scenic views, a charming downtown, access to outdoor activities, and a generally laid-back atmosphere. It’s a sure-fire recipe for a competitive (and pricey) real estate market.

But if you’re looking to invest in a mountain home, and your budget isn’t quite at an Aspen or Big Sky level, I have good news. There are still relatively affordable mountain towns across the U.S., but you have to search outside the more well-known areas. I recently asked Zillow to help dig up data on places where you can buy a home for under $400,000, and the real estate marketplace delivered. Using the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI), or the typical home value in the area, which is “calculated as a weighted average of the middle third of homes in a given region,” Zillow compiled the following list of more affordable mountain towns.

01
of 07
Elkins, West Virginia
A scenic view of a waterfall in West Virginia surrounded by trees
High Falls on Shavers Fork of the Cheat River near Elkins, West Virginia.
Greg Kullman/Wirestock Creators/Adobe Stock
West Virginia is one of those states that remains a well-kept secret. It has an impressive number of outdoor activities—including skiing, hiking, and whitewater rafting—and several charming mountain towns that are tailor-made for relaxing getaways. Elkins, West Virginia, is one such place. Located right on the edge of the Monongahela National Forest and in the Allegheny Mountains, Elkins is a destination where you can experience the best of West Virginia. Go on a rail adventure with the Durbin and Greenbrier Valley Railroad, hike the Allegheny Highlands Trail, and sip on a few local brews at Big Timber Brewing Company. And when you’re ready to start looking for real estate? Expect prices around the $170,000 mark.

02
of 07
Berlin, New Hampshire
Cityscape with a church and buildings near a river
Buildings along the Androscoggin River in Berlin, New Hampshire.
Cappi Thompson/Getty Images
If New England is calling your name, set your home-buying sights on Berlin, New Hampshire. Once a hub for paper production, the city of around 10,000 people is tucked away in the Androscoggin River Valley, and, according to Niche.com, it now has a “sparse suburban feel.” Still, residents have easy access to Jericho Mountain State Park and the White Mountains, so the outdoors are never too far away. Berlin is also a perfect fit for those who enjoy ATVing; ATVs are allowed on paved roads in the city, and every summer, the city hosts Jericho ATV Weekend. One more selling point: the typical home value in Berlin comes in at about $185,000.

03
of 07
Butte, Montana
A street in Butte Montana with historic buildings and parked vehicles mountains visible in the distance
Historic Uptown District in the City of Butte, Montana.
Sanghwan Kim/Getty Images
To find affordable homes in Montana, you’ll need to look outside of Big Sky and Bozeman. Butte is a little further west of both, but it offers a much more palatable real estate market. A former bustling mining town and a Yellowstone filming location, Butte is surrounded by gorgeous public land; the Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest, the largest of its kind in the state, is right next door. The cost of living in Butte is also 8 percent below the national average. That, paired with the typical home value of around $290,000, makes homeownership far more attainable than in many of Montana’s better-known destinations.

04
of 07
Rutland, Vermont
A townscape with churches featuring tall spires and buildings set against a mountain backdrop in Rutland Vermont
The cityscape of Rutland, Vermont.
DenisTangneyJr/Getty Images
Your dream mountain home might be waiting for you in Rutland, Vermont, a small city that sits in the valleys of Pico and Killington mountains in the Stone Valley Region. Yes, that means Killington Resort is only a 25-minute drive away, a huge plus for skiers and snowboarders. When you’re not sending it down the mountain in the winter, you can enjoy the rest of Rutland’s offerings—historic landmarks, live concerts, local shops, parks, hiking trails, swimming holes, and more. It’s a true four-season destination, and one where the typical home value is just south of $300,000.

05
of 07
Pocatello, Idaho
Street with oldstyle buildings and storefronts including a neon Chief sign and trees along the sidewalk in Pocatello Idaho
Businesses in downtown Pocatello, Idaho.
Naya Na/Adobe Stock
Nicknamed the “Gateway to the Northwest,” Pocatello, Idaho, is located in the western foothills of the Rockies, right along the historic Oregon Trail. It’s also only about a two-hour drive from the Tetons, where it’s just about impossible to find a vacation home for under $1 million. Here in Pocatello, however, the typical home value is just under $350,000.  As a resident, you’ll experience a charming small-town atmosphere with dozens of parks, golf courses, cross-country skiing, disc golf, hiking, mountain biking, and the Idaho Museum of Natural History. Niche.com awarded the 58,231-person city an A- for its range of outdoor activities—so you can move to Pocatello knowing you’ll always have something to keep you busy.

06
of 07
Laramie, Wyoming
A rustic water tower and wooden buildings in a Westernstyle setting with a wooden cart in the foreground
Buildings in downtown Laramie, Wyoming.
John Elk/Getty Images
Jackson, Wyoming, may be synonymous with the Wild West, but Laramie is the Cowboy State’s more under-the-radar option for potential home buyers. While it’s not technically in the mountains, the city of around 32,000 people does have the Laramie Mountains and the Vedauwoo Recreation Area to the east and the Snowy Range to the west. When you’re not cozied up in your brand-new home—typical home value is about $380,000—you can spend your days in typical Laramie fashion: hiking, rock climbing, fishing, horseback riding, and breathing in the fresh Wyoming air.

07
of 07
Sonora, California
Aerial view of a small town surrounded by hills and greenery featuring prominent buildings with red roofs
Aerial view of downtown Sonora, California.
adamkaz/Getty Images
You can find affordable mountain living in Sonora, California, a place that only about 5,000 people call home. Located in the Sierra Nevada Foothills, Sonora has everything you’d want in a mountain town: a slower-paced lifestyle, tons of outdoor activities, a strong community feel, and a lower cost of living (it’s 26.8 percent lower than the California average, and the typical home value is about $400,000). Plus, with Sonora as your base camp, you’ll be within driving distance of Yosemite National Park—and you can fish, hike, and camp to your heart’s desire in the Stanislaus National Forest. When you’re craving a bit of city life, San Francisco is just 2.5 hours away.

This Mexican City Might Be the Next Oaxaca
And it's just about two hours from Mexico City.

By Zanny Merullo 
Published on June 21, 2026
In This Article
Best Hotels & Resorts
Best Things to Do
Best Shopping
Best Restaurants
Best Time to Visit
How to Get There
Neighborhoods to Visit
How to Get Around
Decorative papeles picados strung above a colonial street in Puebla Mexico
Views of the historical old town in Puebla, Mexico.
Credit: Julio Etchart/Getty Images
Top 5 Can’t Miss
Stay at Banyan Tree Puebla, which has the best rooftop terrace in the city. 
Go for the mole tasting at El Mural de los Poblanos and sample five different takes on the classic dish. 
Stroll around the Artist Quarter, where troubadours serenade passersby in the evenings. 
Stop by a talavera factory to learn how this local pottery is made. 
Visit in August or September, when Mexico’s national dish, chiles en nogada, is traditionally made and eaten.
In an era of overtourism that has produced strong anti-visitor sentiment in previous “hidden gems,” including Oaxaca, it’s become harder to find a destination with its soul still intact. I spend time in Mexico every year, and after thoroughly exploring Puebla, I was delighted to find it fits the bill.

Puebla, located a little over two hours from Mexico City, is recognized as the first deliberately planned Spanish city in Mexico, built from scratch rather than over an Indigenous site. It was originally called Puebla de los Ángeles (Puebla of the Angels), as the founders claimed they received divine guidance to shape the city as a beacon of Catholicism. To this day, Puebla retains its religious identity through dozens of ornate churches scattered throughout the metropolitan area. 

The destination’s historic and cultural significance doesn’t end there. It was also the site of the victorious Battle of Puebla against French forces on May 5, 1862 (Cinco de Mayo), and it claims many dishes that are intimately tied to Mexican identity. That includes mole, which is also associated with Oaxaca, as well as the national dish: chiles en nogada, or stuffed poblano peppers doused in walnut cream sauce.

According to Puebla native and tour guide Ronnie Cerón, operations coordinator for Dopamina Travel, what makes Puebla stand out is its “sense of place.” Unlike many cities whose identities have faded with years of tourism and gentrification, Puebla “keeps tradition alive through memory, through gastronomy, through love.” It’s also less visited than places like Oaxaca. “When I walk around with international tourists, they ask, ‘Where are the tourists?,’” says Cerón. “Because there are a lot of locals, they feel integrated into the city.”

Here are some of the best ways to spend your time in Puebla. 

Best Hotels & Resorts
Banyan Tree Puebla, a new luxury resort in Mexico
The rooftop pool at Banyan Tree Puebla.
Banyan Tree Puebla
Banyan Tree Puebla
Banyan Tree Puebla, located inside a 19th-century building near the Artist Quarter, was named one of the best resorts in Mexico in 2025 by Travel + Leisure readers. It not only has the most beautiful rooftop terrace in the city—Cerón says it’s “just lovely”— but also a fairy-tale garden, four on-site restaurants, and a spa.

Palacio Julio Hotel
This five-star hotel comprises two 17th-century palaces, complete with vaulted ceilings and a grand chandelier. Other than its proximity to the main square, Palacio Julio Hotel’s greatest appeal is what lies outside its windows: sweeping views of the historic center punctuated by multiple church domes.

Quinta Real Puebla
Quinta Real Puebla is a renovated 16th-century convent in the city’s historic center, blending ancient design details with modern amenities. It has a courtyard with a fountain, a beauty and wellness spa, and a couple of on-site restaurants, including a mezcaleria with some of the finest cocktails in the city.

Casareyna
The highlights of Casareyna are the personal service provided by staff and its courtyard drenched in natural light. Expect rooms that are simple yet tastefully appointed and one of the best restaurants in the city (more on that below). You’ll also have access to a swimming pool, jacuzzi, and spa.

Cartesiano Boutique & Wellness Hotel
Cartesiano Boutique & Wellness Hotel plays peekaboo with pieces of 16th- and 17th-century villas—archways, exposed stone walls, and other features hidden throughout the property. There are two hotel restaurants and a spa that has been recognized for its thorough and high-tech wellness offerings, including a chromotherapy sleep repair bed.

Best Things to Do
Visit the Museo Amparo.
“We have a lot of museums, but my favorite is Museo Amparo,” says Cerón. “There, you can see pre-Hispanic art, colonial art, and contemporary exhibitions. They also have a rooftop terrace that is a really nice place to drink a coffee or have a gin and tonic.”

Check out the Biblioteca Palafoxiana.
In 1646, Catholic bishop Juan de Palafox y Mendoza donated his own collection of books to be accessible to all, which is why the Biblioteca Palafoxiana is recognized as the first public library in the Americas. The beautiful space, with its high ceilings and dark wood carvings, is now a museum and research library, with over 40,000 books.

Tour the historic center.
Puebla’s entire historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for its cultural significance. Start in the main square to see the Puebla Cathedral, and make sure to visit the gilded Chapel of the Rosary. It’s worth taking a guided tour for historical context—local tour companies like Unlimited Experiences and El Viento Tours are good options.

Satisfy your sweet tooth on La Calle de los Dulces.
Puebla’s culinary scene lives up to the hype, but it’s not all about savory eats here. On Avenida 6 Oriente, affectionately called La Calle de los Dulces (Sweets Street), you’ll find shops selling everything from dulce de leche to tortitas de Santa Clara cookies topped with a sweet pepita filling and local sweet potato candy.

Watch the sunset from Mirador de los Fuertes.
“We can’t imagine Puebla without the volcanos,” says Cerón. One of the best places to admire them, he adds, is Mirador de los Fuertes, inside a park home to two historic forts. “You're going to have this beautiful sunset looking at the volcanoes, the old city of Puebla, and the skyscrapers.”

Best Shopping
Artist Quarter
El Barrio del Artista (Artist Quarter) has been a haven for artists since the 1940s. Wander its cobblestone streets and pass open-air studios where painters are at work. “It's one of the most bohemian neighborhoods we have in Puebla,” says Cerón.

Uriarte
If you’ve been to Spain, Puebla’s talavera pottery may look familiar—the designs are rooted in the influence of the Moors who lived on the Iberian Peninsula. In Puebla, talavera has been made in the same way since the 1500s. See this in action during a visit to the Uriarte factory, where you can purchase the pottery, often for a fraction of the price you’d pay in Spain.

Mercado de Sabores
At Mercado de Sabores, you’ll find more than 100 stalls selling local handicrafts and ingredients, as well as dishes like mole, cemitas (sandwiches tucked inside rolls dotted with sesame seeds), traditional sweets, and more. This is one of the best street-food destinations in the city.

La Paz District Boutiques
This district of Puebla, located near Mercado de Sabores, is known for its boutique shops and local fashion designers. Denisse Kuri, for example, collaborates with Indigenous artisans on textiles she then turns into modern clothing for women. Casa Petra, downstairs from Denisse’s shop, sells housewares and decorations, all made in Mexico. 

Callejón de los Sapos
The colorful, quirky Callejón de los Sapos (Alley of the Frogs) is lined with antique shops. Visit on the weekends for the flea market, and you’ll find all kinds of interesting treasures plus the work of local artisans.

Best Restaurants
Four tacos on a plate each filled with seasoned meat and garnished with fresh herbs
A plate of tacos in Puebla City, Mexico.
Glow Images/Getty Images
El Mural de los Poblanos
El Mural de los Poblanos is named for the mural on its walls, the design of local artist Antonio Álvarez Morán. The mural tells the story of Puebla, featuring the faces of important local figures. Make sure to try the mole tasting, which consists of five different versions of the famous dish that was invented here in the city. 

Casona Maria
Hotel Casona Maria is home to an underrated restaurant in its interior courtyard.  Here, executive chef Abdiel Meza curates a menu of dishes that honor Puebla’s Indigenous and European influences, of which there are many. As Cerón puts it, “Our food is the meeting of all the ingredients and the people who arrived in Puebla.”

Casareyna
Casareyna, in the hotel of the same name, has been called one of the best restaurants in Mexico. In addition to a menu of Poblano food, the restaurant also has an extensive wine program, with a focus on local wines.

Augurio
Traditional restaurant Augurio, inside Quinta Esencia Hotel Boutique in the historic center, serves the classics as well as humble offerings, like typical Poblano street food. “We don't have Michelin stars, so that makes our gastronomy really authentic,” says Cerón. “Here, it’s the local people who will judge the food.”

Casa Barroca
One of the draws of Casa Barroca is its building, with vaulted ceilings, exposed stone, and talavera tile floors. As with most restaurants in Puebla, meals here are reasonably priced (most dishes cost under $20), reflecting Cerón’s take: “Fine-dining restaurants can be so expensive, a Mexican cannot pay. Here in Puebla, fine dining is a more local experience.”

Best Time to Visit
Plate of chiles en nogada being held traditional Mexican dish with white sauce pomegranate seeds and embroidered clothing visible
A woman holding platter of chiles en nogada.
Jupiterimages/Getty Images
The best time to visit Puebla depends on how you want to spend your time there. If you come in May, you can see how Cinco de Mayo is celebrated in the city where it originated. Summer, Cerón says, is best for foodies, as the annual Mole Poblano Festival takes place in June, and August and September are the months when you can typically find chiles en nogada. 

He also recommends Puebla for Día de los Muertos in October. During this time, the main square is decorated with altars, skeletons, and marigolds. 

For those who want to take a day trip to hike in Iztaccíhuatl–Popocatépetl National Park—a little over an hour away—winter is ideal, with steady warm temperatures and a photogenic dusting of snow on the volcanoes. 

How to Get There
A highway in a forested area with moving vehicles and surrounding mountains
A road surrounded by hills from the city of Puebla.
Sergio Mendoza Hochmann/Getty Images
Hermanos Serdán International Airport (PBC) is a 40-minute Uber ride from the city center, and it’s a convenient option for those flying from within Mexico. There are also direct flights from Houston via United Airlines. Some hotels, like Banyan Tree, provide transportation from the airport.

Otherwise, the best way to get to Puebla is to fly into Mexico City and take a bus with ADO or Estrella Roja, both of which offer first-class options. There are routes between Benito Juárez International Airport (MEX)—also known as Mexico City International Airport—and the center of Puebla, usually a 2.5-hour ride. 

Neighborhoods to Visit
Centro Historico
The beating heart of Puebla’s UNESCO-listed historic center is the main square, or Zócalo. “Our historic center feels like a small town. The way of life is so cozy, comfortable, [and] slow,” says Cerón.

El Carmen
This neighborhood just south of the center has the same type of colonial architecture and historic feel, but gets fewer visitors than the city center. Visit the neighborhood park or head into the Mercado Melchor Ocampo to sample street food to your heart’s content.  

Barrio del Artista
The Artist Quarter of Puebla isn’t just a shopping destination; it’s also a romantic neighborhood worth spending an afternoon in. You can walk around its postcard-worthy streets, sit in streetside cafes, or rest on its benches shaded by gigantic trees. There are often musicians playing, and plenty of art galleries to wander into.

Cholula
This nearby city is part of the metropolitan area of Puebla and home to an ancient pyramid, which the Spanish eventually built a church on top of after brutally conquering the area. Stop by for a visit to the archaeological site and a meal, or stick around for a nightlife experience more lively than that of downtown Puebla.

How to Get Around
A street in Puebla Mexico showing parked cars and a passing taxi with vibrant colored buildings in the background
Cars and taxis on Alley of the Frogs in the historic city center.
MaxRastello/Getty Images
Cerón says public transportation in Puebla is not the most reliable or convenient, so he highly recommends Uber. You can get a ride around the city for $2 to $10, depending on where you’re going, and a ride from downtown to the airport costs around $20.

Discover Bali's Stunning Landscapes and Luxurious Villas 
Here's where to find the best hotels, restaurants, and things to do in Bali.

By Kathryn Romeyn 
Updated on June 11, 2026
In This Article
Best Hotels & Resorts
Things to Do
Best Shopping
Best Restaurants
Best Time to Visit
How to Get There
Neighborhoods to Visit
How to Get Around
Balinese woman on boat near Ulun Danu Beratan temple, Bedugul, Bali, Indonesia
Credit: Matteo Colombo/Getty Images
As magical destinations go, Bali is definitely up there. There are the awe-inspiring temples in the tens of thousands, and near-daily ceremonies: vivid, multi-sensory, and loud, accompanied by chanting and clanging gamelan. Add to that endless beaches trimmed in aquamarine surf, pulsing with relentlessly curling waves topped with surfers. There are miles and miles of verdant rice paddies, terraced so immaculately they've become iconic. And don't forget canang sari, the prolific flower-laden offerings blessed and placed seemingly everywhere daily on the so-called "Island of Gods."

"From its pristine beaches to lush landscapes, cultural treasures, and thrilling adventures, Bali will resonate with every traveler," Giordano Faggioli, an Indonesia-based hotel manager formerly with Ayana Hospitality, told Travel + Leisure. "Guests can seek relaxation, exploration, spiritual rejuvenation, or adrenaline-pumping pursuits that harmoniously offer an unforgettable experience."

Bali has an energy about it that acts as a siren song to woo-woo wellness practitioners, design buffs, and carousing Gen Z-ers in equal numbers, along with stoked surfers, spiritual pilgrims, yogis, and beach lovers, plus plenty of celebrities and influencers to boot. And the most fulfilling and thrilling Bali holidays include a few locations, so don't stress about picking just one vibe or scene—it's best to combine a few, or two if you're short on time.

"Guests can tailor their Bali experience based on personal preferences," Faggioli said. "My suggestion is to scale the heights of Mount Batur to witness a captivating sunrise over the island’s volcanic terrain. Immerse in the local community and Balinese everyday life at Sukowati market."

Enjoy island time and the locals who are overwhelmingly generous, sweet, and genuine. All factors considered, it's nearly impossible not to leave Bali feeling far better—happier, healthier, and definitely more tan—than when you landed.

Best Hotels & Resorts
Four Seasons Bali at Sayan, Indonesia
Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts
Four Seasons Resort Bali at Sayan
It's obvious you're somewhere special right upon arrival at this John Heah–designed resort. The standalone villas (each with a private pool) and suites have accommodated everyone from the Obamas to Julia Roberts. River rafting, cycling, and other adventurous cultural tours are on offer, but the resort environment—with its pools, flavorful food, and entertainment—is so alluring it's tempting to just relax, too.

Capella Ubud
Capella is one of T+L readers' favorite hotel brands, and its Ubud resort is truly one-of-a-kind. The property's 22 one-bedroom tented and batik-draped retreats and one two-bedroom lodge, a hand-painted Mads Lange restaurant, and even a saltwater pool are set amid Capella Ubud's forested, terraced landscape—not one tree was cut as the whimsical Bill Bensley creations were constructed.

Katamama Suites at Desa Potato Head Bali
An artisanal theme pervades this brick-clad Brutalist boutique hotel that manages to be a quiet respite in the heart of lively Seminyak. It all celebrates Indonesia's rich traditions of craft through a midcentury-esque lens. Tear yourself away from the long turquoise pool to hit the beach, just a few minutes away, or the many shops and restaurants within walking distance.

Como Uma Canggu
This airy modern beachfront resort occupies prime real estate in Canggu, and is within easy walking—or scooting—distance of all the town's hot spots. Hopeful surfers should book lessons with the consummate professionals at Tropicsurf on-site, while the wellness-minded have their choice of Pilates, yoga, a Jungle Sports studio, and a comprehensive spa.

Uluwatu Surf Villas
If paradisiacal views are what you crave, Uluwatu Surf Villas has you covered. The legendary surfers' resort perched above those famously large waves (there's a set of private steps down) offers traditionally Balinese-designed thatched-roof cliff-front villas as well as a collection of newer architectural masterpieces, each one with its own unique tropical modern vibe.

Ayana Villas
Feel like you're the only one in Bali with a stay at Ayana Villas, a resort made up of 73 private villas, each with its own plunge pool. Ocean views, flowering gardens, and utter romance abound at this chic resort, making it an ideal spot for honeymooners to come and bask in that new love glow.

Things to Do
Asian woman at the rice terraces, Bali, Indonesia
Matteo Colombo/Getty Images
Ride a Bike Through Rice Fields
There's no question about the iconic status of Tegallalang, the flawless and highly photogenic rice terraces curving around hillsides and irrigated by the subak system, which has UNESCO status. As good as that hot spot is, the more intimate way to experience the ubiquitous emerald paddies is by bicycle, which many Ubud hotels and tour companies offer, led by local guides.

Try Surfing
Bali's reputation as a surf destination is well earned, thanks to its rich assortment of not only professional-grade waves (see the aquamarine behemoths rolling in like corduroy in Keramas and Uluwatu, where Kelly Slater surfs) but also beginner-level breaks like Baby Padang at Padang Padang Beach and Batu Bolong in Canggu. There are fantastic surf camps and instructors across the island.

Visit Hindu Temples
Bali's transcendent charm is rooted in its tens of thousands of Hindu temples, and there are many worth visiting for a dose of impressively ornate architecture and mystical ambience. Some of the most iconic on the island are Pura Tirta Empul (pura means "temple"), where you can bathe and bless yourself in holy spring waters spouting from carved stone; Pura Besakih, the largest and holiest of them all; and Pura Luhur Uluwatu, the clifftop sea temple where each sunset draws tourists for flashy yet authentic kecak (fire) dances.

Take a Yoga Class at The Yoga Barn
Ubud is associated with all things spiritual and high vibe, with a multitude of yoga studios and movement centers. Practitioners can find more than 180 classes per week at The Yoga Barn, an epicenter of yin, vinyasa, Hatha, and kundalini, plus meditation, sound healing, and ecstatic dance.

Best Shopping
Ceramics by Gaya Ceramic and Design
Gaya Ceramic and Design
Gaya Ceramic
While the founders of this celebrated ceramic design studio are an Italian expat couple, their ultra-skilled team of 100 or so craftsmen is overwhelmingly Indonesian and Balinese. It's impossible to leave the showroom empty-handed, thanks to its proliferation of glamorous handmade dishes and decor.

Canaan x Rou
This petite shop packs a major punch with tightly curated and oftentimes collaborative goods made by Balinese artisans; think placemats, eye-catching brass cutlery, and a plant-dyed shibori clothing collection. Beautiful gifts—for yourself and loved ones back home—include signature Canaan candles, artisanal fans from Central Java, and Cisco & the Sun's wabi-sabi–inspired ceramics.

Magali Pascal
Ethereal, elegant, and earthy womenswear can be found at this Canggu boutique. Magali Pascal opened her first boutique and founded her namesake brand in Bali in 2005. Her style marries an effortless French sensibility with a cool-girl palette, ideal for island holidays.

Drifter
You don't need to be a pro in the waves to embark on a spree at this beloved surf shop. A reclaimed joglo house holds dozens of slick, technicolor surfboards—finely crafted by sought-after shapers—along with Drifter's own brand of art-emblazoned tees, swimwear, original artwork, boho jewelry, and ocean-themed books, among other creations.

Best Restaurants
View from inside Zest in Bali
Zest
Kaum
With a name meaning "tribe" in Bahasa Indonesia, Kaum is a concept born of its culinary team's deep exploration of Indonesia's super diverse archipelago, regional ingredients, and traditional cooking techniques (fishing and spear hunting, to name a few). A sampling of fiery sambals is a great way to start feasting on rich regional dishes made of specialty ingredients sourced as locally as possible.

Zest
It's not too extreme an exaggeration to call Ubud a mecca for vegans, and this chic, plant-powered restaurant is like the high temple in the lush jungle. Zest appropriately hugs a living frangipani tree and offers up colorful, organic fare like jackfruit steaks, pizzas, and cassava fettuccini alongside a lively community and a menu of creative, island-grown cocktails and tonics.

Hujan Locale
Casually elegant and tucked away like a well-kept secret amid Ubud's busy streets, this eatery is a perfect blend of a warung (a basic Indonesian cafe or small restaurant) and a fine dining restaurant. Sit near one of many open windows for views of a classic Balinese neighborhood while sipping vibrant cocktails like Pala Gin Mojitos.

Chef's Table at Sokasi
Intimate dinners at Sokasi—the curvaceous bamboo pavilion perched above the rushing Ayung River at the Four Seasons in Sayan—are all about preserving the island's time-intensive culinary heritage. Arrive early for a peek at the pig roasting over a coconut wood fire before tucking into rich, forgotten recipes featuring flavors like wild ginger and klengis (an extract from hand-made coconut oil).

Cuca Restaurant Bali
Tapas in Indonesia sounds random, but dreamed up and prepared with quality produce and products sourced from the archipelago by chef Kevin Cherkas (whose CV includes several Michelin three-star restaurants), it's flawless. The Chef Tasting Meal at Cuca is a favorite at this vegetarian-friendly fine-dining spot. And though its ingredients evoke Indonesia, the plates—which include everything from BBQ octopus and Turkish meatballs to crispy fried chicken—are all over the map.

Best Time to Visit
Drone shot of cliffs of Bali
Daniel Gorostieta/Travel + Leisure
The best time to visit Bali is during both the summer holiday months and the local festive season. One of the biggest holidays of the year is Nyepi, which happens in March and involves fantastical parades of men and boys hauling ogoh-ogoh (huge handmade demon dolls) the night before a 24-hour silent day, on which even the airport falls quiet, and planes don't take off or land, and the use of electricity and vehicles is forbidden. For that period, tourists must stay on the grounds of their accommodations, but it's a beautiful opportunity to experience Balinese culture as well as epic stargazing. Surfers will find the best waves on the west coast of Bali from May to October, at which point the winds shift and it improves on the eastern side.

"Being an equatorial getaway boasting a consistently delightful climate, this destination attracts globetrotters from across the world, regardless of whether it's the dry or rainy season," Faggioli shared. "Nevertheless, my ultimate preference rests with the period spanning from June to August. During these months, the sun graces the skies daily, and the weather is very nice."

Bali doesn't experience four seasons in the same way we do. Instead, there are just two: rainy and dry. When it rains, it really pours, but there can also be beautiful days during that humid period, from November to March. April to October tends to be far drier and equally hot, though nights can feel quite cool. Daytime temperatures hover in the high 70s and 80s Fahrenheit year-round.

How to Get There
Plane: Because Bali is an island, the most practical way to get there is by plane. Visitors will fly into its one international airport, Denpasar-Ngurah Rai International Airport (DPS), which services flights from all over the world.

Ferry: There are also plentiful ferries that travel from the mainland of Indonesia to Bali. See all the available ferry terminals and times here.

Cruise: Another option is to book a cruise that stops in Bali as one of its ports of call. Several cruise lines, including Royal Caribbean and Celebrity Cruises, make stops here.

Neighborhoods to Visit
Exterior of Canaan at Potato Head in Bali
Canaan at Potato Head
Seminyak
This is Bali's best-known beach neighborhood, and without a doubt, one of its busiest. Here, you'll find countless places to shop, eat, and drink along its vibrant, crowded streets, not to mention hundreds of deluxe villas and many luxury hotels. Partying isn't confined to after-dark hours—beach clubs like Potato Head and Ku De Ta are popular at all times of day and night.

Canggu
Think of Canggu as the newer Seminyak—super hip and, in recent years, where a burst of development has occurred, giving this seaside beach town plenty of cool little boutiques. Plus, loads of eateries and bars are helmed by chefs from around the world, bringing not only international flavors but also aesthetics.

Ubud
Ever since Elizabeth Gilbert's "Eat Pray Love" threw Ubud (pronounced oo-bood) into the spotlight, it's become almost every tourist's definition of Bali. That's ironic considering the island is known for its beaches, and this busy, sprawling town full of yoga studios, vegan cafes, shops, spas, and markets is a 30-minute motorbike ride from the nearest stretch of sand. Still, it's probably the most popular stop in Bali, a great jumping-off point for temple visits, hikes (Mt. Batur is lovely at sunrise), visits with healers, coffee (kopi) tastings, and a serious dose of culture.

Uluwatu
If you surf, you've already heard of Uluwatu. Besides its epic waves, the southwesternmost tip of Bali is famed for Pura Uluwatu, the clifftop Hindu temple where monkeys cause mischief as sarong-clad visitors take in panoramic sunsets. Uluwatu and its neighboring surf towns of Padang Padang and Bingin are more low-key than Canggu, with more dramatically beautiful beaches (many of which require a decent number of steps to access) and a laid-back but luscious restaurant and cafe scene.

Nusa Lembongan
This tiny island off the southeastern coast is technically part of Bali (along with the even teenier Nusa Ceningan and much larger but less developed Nusa Penida), but it's about 20 years behind developmentally, which means it's a bit closer to the storied Bali of yore. Still, there are already plenty of Instagrammable hotels and eateries here, so if you're keen for some scuba diving, snorkeling, or more surf, it makes a fun spinoff for a few days (the fast boat from Sanur or Serangan takes about 30–45 minutes).

How to Get Around
Motorbike: Bali does not have a public transit system in the Western sense—there are some buses, but they are not reliable or advised. Instead, the ubiquitous motorbikes that flood every street (and sometimes sidewalk) are the primary mode of transportation. There are plentiful rental services to assist in finding the bike for you.

Taxi: If the idea of riding a motorbike stresses you out (and it should a bit, as the experience is not for the timid), there are plentiful local taxis for hire.

Private car: There are also abundant private cars with gracious Balinese drivers who will happily be on call to ferry you around the island, many of whom double as casual tour guides.

Rental cars: Almost every rental car service operates in Bali and is available from the airport. If you plan to see a lot of the area, it is a good idea to rent your own car (or hire a private driver to take you around as above).

7 of the best U.K. summer festivals for families
Music festivals in the UK are doing more than ever to cater to all interests and ages. Here are this summer’s family-friendly highlights.

ByDom Tulett and Daniela Toporek
Last updated June 21, 2026




This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK).
Music festivals are doing more than ever to cater to all interests and ages. Younger audiences are often won over purely by the fact that attendance typically involves camping, glamping or pitching up in a caravan — an opportunity to sleep out in the wild. But the UK’s best festivals also provide an endless roster of activities, workshops and experiences to help families bond and create lasting memories. From chilled countryside escapes to adrenaline-sparking coastal adventures, here are the golden tickets for this summer.

1. Camp Bestival
Best for: big music acts
When: 30 July to 2 August

Set in the grounds of Lulworth Castle, Dorset’s award-winning festival always has a solid line-up, from Fatboy Slim to Bastille and Billy Ocean. Away from the main stages, there’s the world’s biggest bouncy castle, mud kitchens and activities such as kids’ talent shows, craft workshops and sensory gardens. At the Orchestra of Objects, children can even invent their own musical instruments from junk.

Highlight: Dressing up for seaside-themed fancy dress competition.

2. Green Man
Best for: connecting with nature
When: 20-23 August

Backdropped by Bannau Brycheiniog (the Brecon Beacons National Park), the campsite at Green Man opens three days before the action starts, giving families the opportunity to enjoy a week-long break in rural Wales. After evenings spent dancing to the likes of Brit Award winners Wolf Alice and indie icons Wilco, welcome each new day with a family sunrise yoga session before wandering over to Einstein’s Garden for scientific installations, art and wildlife walks. Older kids can try their hand at film-making, crafting and mastering circus skills in the ‘Somewhere’ zone.

Highlight: The closing fireworks display and ritual burning of the Green Man sculpture to symbolise rebirth in the natural world.


At the Wilderness Festival in Oxfordshire, the Family Field is full of games, theatre and workshops for all ages.
Photograph by Sarah Louise Bennett
3. Wilderness Festival
Best for: sparking creativity
When: 30 July to 2 August

Set within the 5,000-acre Cornbury Park in Oxfordshire, Wilderness Festival has a suitably retro music line-up for parents this year, including the Scissor Sisters and a special takeover by Annie Lennox. There’s also a dedicated Family Field packed with activities to spark the imagination and inspire creativity. Younger ravers can attend the regular storytelling sessions or craft workshops to build masterpieces out of natural materials; for older kids, there are slime-making and circus workshops, comic-drawing sessions and poetry classes, plus woodland theatre. And when parents want to attend a gig solo or visit the Lakeside Spa & Sauna, there’s a popular nanny service for the little ones.

Highlight: Hands-on radio and podcasting tutorials with experienced producers for budding broadcasters.

4. Camp Kindling
Best for: bonding adventures
When: 21-24 August

Exclusively for families, this Kent favourite prides itself on being more like a summer camp than a festival. Over 100 adventurous activities are on offer throughout the ancient woodland setting. For a quieter moment away from the zorbing, raft-building and beekeeping, grown-ups can take advantage of on-site childcare and nip to the adults-only wellness sanctuary.

Highlight: Join a patrol — the Kindling version of a house at school — and work with new friends to compete for the Kindling Cup.


At Deer Shed music festival, there’s no designated kids’ area — the whole event, dedicated to discovery and expanding younger children’s minds, is accessible.
Photograph by James Drury
5. Deer Shed
Best for: inspiring young minds
When: 24-26 July

The landscaped fields that host Deer Shed are part of a working farm close to Ripon in North Yorkshire. There’s no designated kids’ area — the whole event, dedicated to discovery and expanding younger children’s minds, is accessible. Children can see where imagination leads listening to fireside stories and create bug houses for creepy-crawlies at eco-friendly workshops. Sleaford mods, Say She She and Everything Everything are headlining this year; for the smallest ravers, there’s the blackout tent hosting a toddler ‘nightclub’.

Highlight: DJing classes, to help aspiring kids on their journey towards festival headlining.


Food is the main attraction at Cornwall's Rock Oyster Festival.
Photograph by the Rock Oyster Festival, Caitlin Mogridge
6. Rock Oyster Festival
Best for: water babies
When: 23-26 July

Making the most of its Cornish coastal location, just a rock’s throw from Padstow, Rock Oyster offers an armada of water-based activities, from surfing lessons to a pirate school. This year’s impressive musical line-up includes Groove Armada and Kool & the Gang. Food plays a major role here, too, with celebrity chef masterclasses and a cookery school for kids.

Highlight: A model-making workshop with Aardman, the creative brains behind Wallace and Gromit

7. Deva Fest
Best for: funfair fans
When: 6-9 August

Taking its title from the Roman name for nearby Chester, this festival is set in fields overlooked by Cholmondeley Castle. It gives older children a glimpse of life 2,000 years ago with archery, axe-throwing and bushcraft sessions. Younger revellers will enjoy the games and shows led by a team from Chester Zoo, covering topics such as the science behind animal poo. Deva Fest is friendly on the wallet, too, with free fairground rides hoovering up the daylight hours, before Ronan Keating and Jessie J take to the main stage.

Highlight: The Grand Cavalcade troupe of performers leading explosive science experiments, madcap storytelling and interactive workshops.

The best beaches for a weekend getaway—just a train ride away from NYC
Ocean air and uncrowded shorelines can be found less than two hours from the Big Apple. Here are six of the best coastal escapes.

People enjoy the sun and sand at the beach on Fire Island, New York. This car-free stretch of Atlantic coastline just an hour from New York City.
WoodysPhotos, Shutterstock
ByMichele Herrmann
Published June 18, 2026




It’s no secret that summer is one of the most popular times to visit New York City. But with average high temperatures sitting in the 80s and stifling humidity, some travelers may want a break from the Big Apple. 

While popular seaside spots like the Hamptons require advanced planning, several beaches are just a train ride away and offer historic sites, nature, and small-town charm along with uncrowded shorelines. 

(Antoni Porowski's guide to New York City)

Here are six of the best beaches not far from New York City. 

Jones Beach State Park, Long Island
Travel time from NYC: Just under two hours by train
Known for: Outdoor concert venue and Fourth of July fireworks show

A woman sits along the Jones Beach Boardwalk and looks out towards the shore. Urban planner Robert Moses brought Art Deco design to directly to the beaches of Jones Beach State Park.
Alejandra Villa Loarca/Newsday RM, Getty Images
An early project by influential New York City urban planner Robert Moses, Jones Beach State Parkcombines the recreational activities of a city park with 6.5 miles of white-sand beaches along the Atlantic Ocean and Long Island’s south shore.

“You have various activities throughout Jones Beach that you could partake in one day,” says George Gorman Jr., regional director of New York’s Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation on Long Island. “And then come back a second day, and it would be like a new experience.”

Besides its picturesque coastline, Jones Beach is known for concerts The Northwell at Jones Beach Theater, an outdoor amphitheater, hosts top performers such as James Taylor, Rod Stewart and the Dave Matthews Band, while The Jones Beach Bandshell, which is directly along the boardwalk, presents free summer events, such as Fourth of July fireworks and the FourLeaf Air Show. 

Swimmers have lots of options, from designated on-duty lifeguard spots (if you’re driving, park in field 6) to the calm waters of Zach’s Bay, located on the other side of Ocean Parkway. Additionally, the park’s two historic bathhouses—West Bathhouse Pool and East Bathhouse—are great alternatives for visitors who want to avoid the sand. At press time, East Bathhouse was set to reopen in summer 2026, after an extensive restoration.

Outdoors lovers may want to stop by Jones Beach Energy & Nature Center to learn about the area’s nature-based energy sources, such as wave action, in the ecosystems; take guided nature walks; or try the zipline and obstacle course at WildPlay Jones Beach.

(These Black resort towns are still refuges today)

After working up an appetite, stop by the Boardwalk Café for a quick bite (or ice cream) or head across the bay to restaurants like Dirty Taco + Tequila in Wantagh, for a lively atmosphere and street-style tacos, or Salt on The Water in Merrick for dockside dining. About a seven-minute drive, The  Buoy Bar serves American classics at lots of outdoor tables with views across Point Lookout.

Getting there: From Penn Station or Grand Central Madison in Manhattan, take the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR) from Babylon Branch to the Freeport Station. From there, head downstairs to catch the Nassau Inter-County Express northbound bus to the beach. With a seasonal, nonstop schedule, the n88xpress makes two stops along the beach at: West Bathhouse, which is around 17 minutes and near the park’s boardwalk, and Central Mall a main dining, retail and rec hub that’s about a minute away. (Note: The current 2026 schedule does not include East Bathhouse.)

Where to stay: Opened in 1929, Jones Beach Hotel is tucked away in a quiet neighborhood bordering Cedar Creek Park and offers charming vintage-style rooms and an upscale Italian restaurant.

Fire Island, New York 
Travel time from NYC: An hour by train, plus a half-hour ferry
Known for: A rare maritime holly forest and LGBTQ history

A view of Fire Island, New York, captured on the top of the historic Fire Island Lighthouse. Majority of the barrier island is protected land, with seven miles of federally designated wilderness where you can explore ancient maritime forests and untouched dunes.
Jay Gao, Shutterstock
A primarily car-free getaway, Fire Island is a 32-mile thin barrier island off of Long Island, sprinkled with 17 distinctive communities, historic maritime sites, and miles of sand dune-dotted beaches and salt marshes. It also coincides with Fire Island National Seashore, a National Park Service site established in 1969 to protect the island’s coastal resources and prevent overdevelopment.

The island’s unofficial capital is Ocean Beach, a singles and family-friendly spot buzzing with a sweeping beachfront and homey restaurants like Rachel's Fire Island Restaurant & Bakery offering sit-down meals and sweet treats like their famous crumb cake to go.

In Kismet, check out the Fire Island Lighthouse, the largest in the state, with views of the New York City skyline, the Atlantic Ocean, and Long Island’s bays. The Fire Island Pedicab takes visitors there and to Robert Moses State Park, located at Fire Island’s western end.

Nature lovers can’t go wrong with Sailors Haven’s Sunken Forest, a “globally rare” maritime holly forest home to many tree species protected by a double dune system. Alexcy Romero, superintendent with the Fire Island National Seashore, notes that a boardwalk runs through the forest. Visitors can also book ranger-led tours. 

Cherry Grove and Fire Island Pines (“The Pines” to locals) neighborhoods are steeped in LGBTQ+ history. In Cherry Grove, beloved Cherry’s On the Bay has been drawing fans to its drag brunch for years, while The Pines has long been a social hub with a pool club, pavilion, and the harborside restaurant, The Blue Whale. 

(Must-see LGBTQ-friendly destinations for every kind of traveler)  

Getting there: Take the LIRR to one of three stations on the Montauk Branch, then take a shuttle bus or taxi to one of three ferries. Fire Island Ferries services the western end and operates Fire Island Water Taxi. Sayville Ferry Service connects to the central and eastern communities. Davis Park Ferry sails to the easternmost areas.

Where to stay: Locals say Watch Hill, on the western edge of the Otis Pike Fire Island High Dune Wilderness, makes a good base for campers. Non-campers can try a vacation rental or book rooms at The Grove Hotel, which has a pool and a packed calendar of events, or The Palms Hotel Fire Island, whose cottage-style décor makes a serene backdrop for rest and relaxation.

Long Beach, New York
Travel time from NYC: Under an hour by train
Known for: Surfing and a bustling boardwalk 

Surfers walk along New York's Long Beach at sunset as waves crash in the background. The south shore hurricane swells makes this a premier spot for seasoned pros.
Scott Heaney, Adobe Stock
This “City by the Sea” on Long Island’s south shore draws travelers and surfers with 3.5 miles of prime beach and a 2.1-mile historic boardwalk. Surfers typically paddle out from Azores and Lincoln Boulevard Beach, but also follow a rotating surf schedule set by the city.

Outside of catching waves and sun on the beach, there’s plenty to explore. In West End, historic 1920s bungalows and boardwalk cottages set the scene for laidback summer strolls. On Saturdays, locals and visitors explore “Arts In The Plaza,” an arts market that runs through late October.

West Beech Street bustles with bars, cafés, and surf shops. Popular spots include The Merrow, an Irish pub-style restaurant; Lost At Sea, in intimate space serving seafood and craft cocktails; and Speakeasy, a local hangout specializing in craft beers. 

Right off the boardwalk, Lido Kosher Delicatessen dishes up comfort foods, while  Riptides 11561 fries up fish and chips. Walk up to Marvel Frozen Dairy, a Long Beach institution that’s been scooping ice cream and whipping up milkshakes since 1951.

Getting there: Take the LIRR Long Beach Branch line from Penn Station, Grand Central Madison, or Brooklyn’s Atlantic Terminal to the Long Beach Station. (You may need to transfer at LIRR’s Jamaica station, depending on the day’s schedule). To access the beach, visitors must purchase a 10-day or seasonal pass.

Where to stay: The Allegria Hotel is Long Island’s only oceanfront accommodation. It has a rooftop pool with sea views and an airy restaurant and bar serving new American-style cuisine. 

Sandy Hook, New Jersey
Travel time from NYC: 50 minutes by ferry
Known for: Military history and America’s oldest-operating lighthouse

A row of Fort Hancock's historic homes in Sandy Hook, New Jersey. Fort Hancock is a former U.S. Army coastal artillery base that defended New York Harbor from 1895 to 1974.
andykazie, Getty Images
At the northern tip of the New Jersey shore, in Middletown Township, Sandy Hook comprises a barrier peninsula with seven miles of sand and six public beaches. It’s also home to the largest stand of American holly trees on the East Coast.

But the standout here is Sandy Hook Lighthouse, the oldest-operating lighthouse in the U.S., built in 1764. National Park Service rangers lead public tours up through the nine-rung ladder to the lantern room, where visitors can imagine the area during the Revolutionary War. The site includes the decommissioned Fort Hancock, whose history predates the Civil War and is now a National Historic Landmark, together with the lighthouse.

Getting there: Seastreak offers seasonal ferry service between New York City and Sandy Hook Beach.

Where to stay: The SummerHouse, in Highlands, offers cozy cottages with a courtyard. Beachwalk at SeaBright, in Seabright, has a variety of rooms overlooking the beach and a pool. Campers can book spots at Camp Gateway, a hike-in, tent-only campground across from Horseshoe Cove in the Gateway National Recreation Area.

Rockaway Beach, New York
Travel time from NYC: About an hour and a half by ferry or subway
Best known for: Surfing and a wildlife refuge

Wildflowers at the west pond at the Jamaica Bay National Wildlife Refuge in Queens, New York. The protected wetland has seen more than 330 bird species pass through over the last two decades.
Stubblefield Photography, Shutterstock
Made famous by rock band, The Ramones, Rockaway Beach is the only legally designated surfing beach within New York City. Besides surfing, visitors have lots of options, from browsing the seasonal Edgemere Farm market in Far Rockaway to birdwatching along the salt marshes atJamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge.

“We have seven miles of beach, and the vast majority of it is open to the public,” says Elizabeth Walsack, administrator of Rockaway and Broad Channel for the NYC Department of Parks & Recreation. “There’s so much activity on the boardwalk, including pickleball and handball courts and basketball, every sport you could play here. We even have a labyrinth, where you walk and meditate, just off the beach.”

Within Queens’ Rockaway Peninsula, the 5.5-mile boardwalk has three designated surfing areas—Beach 90th Street to Beach 92nd Street, Beach 67th Street to Beach 69th Street, and Beach 110th Street to Beach 111th Street. Visitors who want to learn how to surf can sign up for lessons with New York Surfing School, Locals Surf School, or Sierra Surf School.

After working up an appetite, head to Beach 97th, along Rockaway Beach Boulevard. The largest concession has eight food stands, with vendors selling everything from ceviche to wood-fired pizza, and poke bowls. Popular sit-down restaurants in the area include dockside Similan on the Bay for familiar Thai favorites and sea views, or Tacoway Beach, a colorful spot serving fish tacos in Far Rockaway.

Getting there: NYC Ferry’s Rockaway-Soundview route connects to the Bronx, Manhattan, and Brooklyn, on weekend and weekday schedules. From the subway, take MTA’s A Queens-Bound line (marked as Far Rockaway) to Broad Channel. On summer weekends, the S (Rockaway Park Shuttle train) operates between Rockaway Boulevard and Rockaway Park Beach 116 St.  

Where to stay: The Rockaway Hotel + Spa offers nightly rates as well as long-stay residences, with some water-view rooms. The hotel features a spa with several massage services, a heated pool, and wet and dry saunas.

Asbury Park, New Jersey
Travel time from NYC: About an hour and a half by train
Best known for: Vibrant art and music scenes, with a lively boardwalk

Located on the boardwalk in New Jersey, Asbury Park Convention Hall is known for its rock and roll history.
Vincent DeMilio, Shutterstock
This small beach town is big on the arts. “Asbury Park has a little bit of everything, that’s [what] makes it so unique compared to some of our other shore towns,” said Matthew Whelan, executive director of the Asbury Park Chamber of Commerce. “I like to tell people there’s always music somewhere in Asbury Park.”

Music lovers shouldn’t miss the Stone Pony where The Boss honed his chops as a young performer and now serves as center stage for summer concerts. Quirky Wonder Bar is a fun spot for discovering new performers.

The beach town’s namesake Asbury Boardwalk offers the quintessential summer experience. It’s lined with boutiques and ice cream shops and located near the Paramount Theater & Convention Hall and Asbury Splash Park. On the Sunset Pavilion’s side of the boardwalk, admire colorful murals commissioned by the Wooden Walls Project and try your luck at Madame Marie, a fun longtime fortune-telling booth. 

Silverball Retro Arcade is a hub for families, with antique pinball machines and classic video games along the boardwalk. Dining options range from the seafood-focused Iron Whale to Ethiopian and Dominican Ada’s Gojjo. Husband-and-wife run pizzeria Talula’s is a good option for families with kids. 

Getting there: From Penn Station, take NJ Transit North Jersey Coast Line train to the Asbury Park Station. A badge is required to access the beach.

Where to stay: Boutique-style St. Lauren Social Club is an 21+ facility (with just 20 rooms, a restaurant, and a lounge housed in an 1886 building. The Asbury Hotel is a fun spot attached to Asbury Lanes, a vintage bowling alley, with lots of shows and events. Century-old Berkeley Oceanfront Hotel has hosted world leaders and celebrities. Asbury Ocean Club Hotel offers tastefully decorated rooms steps from the boardwalk.  

Michele Herrmann is a food and travel writer who splits her time between New York and New England.
